                                          Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) patterns (EBSPs) are an excellent case study for the use of few-shot
                                          transfer learning toward accelerating analysis of electron diffraction data. The scanning electron microscope
                                   (SEM)-based method involves the capture of 2D diffraction patterns produced from an incident electron beam
                                             scattering, diffracting, and escaping from a well-polished ‘bulk’ ­sample43. The collected diffraction patterns con-
                                           tain significant structural and chemical information and are similar to those collected in other techniques such
                                         as convergent beam electron diffraction (CBED)44,45. Despite the vast amount of information in the patterns,
                                       conventional EBSD has primarily focused on determining the three-dimensional orientation of individual grains
                                         in crystalline ­materials43,46–48. Furthermore, the commercial technique typically relies on Hough-based indexing
                                     with a look-up table of interplanar angles constructed from the set of selected reflectors for phases specified by
                                       the ­user49. This generally allows for phase differentiation of sufficiently distinct crystal ­structures50–52, but the
                                        process remains susceptible to structural ­misclassification53–55. Improvements to phase differentiation have been
                                    proposed and developed including dictionary ­indexing56–59, spherical ­indexing60–62, and more recently machine
                                                 ­learning63. While each offers significant advantages over the Hough-based method, these tools continue to require
                                     assumptions about the number of phases and/or their structure. For example, the dictionary-based approach
                                         requires simulation of a “master” pattern for each potential phase and every experimental pattern is matched
                                          against a dictionary of simulated patterns for all potential ­phases56. The highest similarity match is selected as the
                                 most likely phase and orientation. Another available solution to phase differentiation is combining an electron
                                        backscattered pattern (EBSP) with information from energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) or wavelength
                                           dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (WDS)64–66. While these have been adopted commercially, the singular EBSP is still
                                      analyzed with the Hough-based method and an expert user is required to evaluate the plausibility of returned
                                      matches. Applications using hand-drawn lines overlaid on individual Kikuchi diffraction patterns have been
                                     developed for determining the Bravais lattice or point group; however, they remain limited by at least one of the
                                         following: analysis time per pattern, the need for an expert crystallographer, or necessitating multiples of the
                                 same diffraction pattern with different SEM ­settings67. Clearly, there remains a need for a rapid EBSP classifica-
                                         tion tool capable of functioning with one EBSD pattern while remaining suitable for even the most novice user.
                                            Recently, the EBSD community has begun to explore the use of convolutional neural networks as a foun-
                                      dation for addressing modern EBSD ­challenges16,68–70. Despite the marked advances these works have made,
                                       the requirements for ­simulating71 or collecting experimental diffraction patterns from a significant number of
                                         materials and crystallographic orientations remains a limiting factor. In this work, we test the validity of few-shot
                                           transfer learning, starting from ImageNet weights, applied to classify EBSPs to one of six space groups. Herein,
                                      space group refers to the symmetry group of a configuration in three-dimensional space. We compare the time
                                         to converge, the individual kernels (weights of the neurons), activation maps, and the performance of models
                                        trained from scratch or by transfer learning. Though there has been considerable progress on interpretability
                                          of machine learning systems, mostly in the field of eXplainable AI (XAI)72, fully understanding the internal
                                 mechanisms of deep neural networks is still an area of active ­research15,73. Visualization of the most similar
                                      weights each model independently learned, their respective activation maps, and Shapley values can increase
                                     understanding of how the artificial intelligence models accomplishes its task. Building these XAI foundations
                                    can increase trust in the model’s later predictions and help identify when the prediction is incorrect. In addition

    OPEN Efficient few‑shot machine learning
           for classification of EBSD patterns

                        Kevin Kaufmann1, Hobson Lane2,3, Xiao Liu4 & Kenneth S. Vecchio1,4*

                      Deep learning is quickly becoming a standard approach to solving a range of materials science
                              objectives, particularly in the field of computer vision. However, labeled datasets large enough to
                               train neural networks from scratch can be challenging to collect. One approach to accelerating the
                              training of deep learning models such as convolutional neural networks is the transfer of weights
                        from models trained on unrelated image classification problems, commonly referred to as transfer
                              learning. The powerful feature extractors learned previously can potentially be fine-tuned for a new
                                classification problem without hindering performance. Transfer learning can also improve the results
                             of training a model using a small amount of data, known as few-shot learning. Herein, we test the
                             effectiveness of a few-shot transfer learning approach for the classification of electron backscatter
                               diffraction (EBSD) pattern images to six space groups within the 4/m32/m point group. Training
                             history and performance metrics are compared with a model of the same architecture trained from
                              scratch. In an effort to make this approach more explainable, visualization of filters, activation maps,
                       and Shapley values are utilized to provide insight into the model’s operations. The applicability to
                             real-world phase identification and differentiation is demonstrated using dual phase materials that are
                            challenging to analyze with traditional methods.


                          Data science-based methods to materials development and analysis have gained great popularity in recent
                                       ­years1–13. Deep learning algorithms are of significant interest owing to their excellent performance without sig-
                                  nificant feature engineering, and the ubiquity of these methods will likely continue owing to the outperformance
                                of systems directly designed by humans. While often difficult to assess how and why these ‘black box algorithms’
                               are capable of performing these tasks, these methods can provide significant value or spark new ­insights14,15.
                              Application of these tools to image-based tasks in materials science has proved to be useful for ­classification16–19,
                                 ­segmentation20–22, and other ­objectives23–25. While deep learning provides significant opportunities for the
                          advancement of materials science, robust application of these tools often requires much larger datasets than are
                                  typically available within the materials science community. Utilizing the knowledge deep neural networks have
                              learned from other domains offers an opportunity to develop models in these domains, where data is sparse and
                               further collection and labeling could be slow or ­tedious26–28.
                               Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are a class of deep learning models that have proven effective for
                              analyzing image ­data29. Before a CNN can be applied to a given task, it must learn to assign importance (learnable
                             weights and biases) to various aspects of the image that maximize the network’s differentiation capabilities. Two
                              general strategies exist for training convolutional neural networks: (1) the weights can be randomly initialized,
                             or (2) the weights can be transferred from a model pre-trained on a separate but related task, often in a nearby
                         domain with significantly more data, and then refined for the current objective. The first approach, commonly
                                referred to as "training from scratch", requires a large dataset to avoid overfitting and perform robustly on new,
                               real-world examples. The second approach, referred to as "transfer learning", can significantly reduce the number
                                of training examples required, accelerate the training process, and retain or exceed the performance garnered
                           by training from ­scratch27,30–32. The transfer learning method is motivated by the human ability to intelligently
                              apply previously learned knowledge to solve new problems faster or with better ­solutions33. Despite the potential,
                          knowledge transfer from a given source domain is not guaranteed to improve performance in the target domain
                         and can in fact hinder ­performance26,32. Furthermore, one of the requirements to use this approach is that the
                           images in the new domain must conform to the processed shape and structure determined at the outset of the
                             previous training. For models pre-trained on ­ImageNet34, a library of over one million images labeled with one
                            thousand classes, the expected input is usually 299 × 299 pixels with 3-channels (one each for RGB). When dealing

The most common image simulation method is the multislice algorithm, and there is no shortage of codes imple-
menting it 8–19, though the degree of support and documentation varies widely. Implementations have remained
largely similar for a good while, apart from some iterative improvements. One significant recent development
has been to use one (or more) graphics processing units (GPUs) for accelerating the calculations. In terms of
methods, the most important recent advancement is the development of the PRISM algorithm, which massively
accelerates scanning TEM (STEM) simulations20.

Here, we present the abTEM code, which is a new multislice image simulation package created to seamlessly
merge DFT and other atomistic modeling methods with electron scattering simulations, providing a much eas-
ier way of performing TEM simulations with an ab initio description of bonding. We have implemented both
the multislice and PRISM algorithms to simulate all the standard imaging modes.

abTEM is further distinguished from existing codes by its pure Python implementation and focus on user extend-
ability. We show that thanks to the effective utilization of open-source libraries, the performance of abTEM is as
good or even better compared to similar codes implemented in programming languages that have traditionally
been considered superior in performance, such as C or Fortran. abTEM already includes fast GPU implementa-
tions of all of its algorithms on widely used NVidia GPUs, and support for products from AMD is planned for the
near future.

abTEM  is an open-source  project under  the GPLv3  license, and we welcome  contributions  via our open
Github  repository21. Documentation and code examples  are found  online. The code was announced  at  the
M&M 2020 meeting22, and it supersedes and replaces our earlier PyQSTEM code6.

This article is organized as follows: in Section 2, we discuss the physical methodology behind abTEM, includ-
ing  its  implementation  of  the  multislice  electron  scattering  algorithm, IAM and ab  initio  potentials,  the
PRISM algorithm, and inelastic and thermal diffuse scattering. Next, in Section 3 we give brief remarks on our
implementation details, followed by illustrative code examples. In Section 4, we discuss in turn programmatic
modularity, dependencies and  availability, interactive dashboards, and  finally GPU memory management. We
then turn to actual use cases in Section 5, providing novel results on systems that highlight how easy it is to use
ab initio electrostatic potentials and how fast and efficient abTEM is. Finally, we end with a brief conclusion in
Section 6, including features that we plan to develop next.

2 Methods and algorithms
2.1 Multislice
The multislice algorithm can be used to simulate any kind of TEM measurement: what differs is only how the
input wave function of the electron probe is defined and how the scattered exit wave function is detected. Since
the multislice algorithm is conceptually quite simple and discussed in detail elsewhere8, we provide only a brief
sketch of the method here.

In the multislice algorithm, the specimen electrostatic potential is divided into thin slices along the beam propa-
gation direction (which by abTEM convention  is the z axis). Scattering  is calculated by alternating so-called
phase object transmission through each slice with propagation of the wave to the next. For an electron wave 𝜓n
impinging on slice number n, this can be expressed as

                               ψ( n +1) = p * (ψ n t n ),

where p  is the Fresnel free-space propagator, * represents the convolution operation, and the transmission
function tn is defined as

where i is the imaginary unit, σ is the interaction constant dependent on the electron wavelength λ, and

                                                                    z n +∆ z

is the n’th projected potential slice with thickness ∆z.

The convolution is conveniently calculated as a multiplication in Fourier space via a succession of a forward
and an inverse Fourier transform. Another Fourier transform  is needed  to bandwidth-limit the transmission
function and the Fresnel propagator to 2/3 of the Nyquist frequency to avoid aliasing artifacts8.

The  Fourier transforms  are  carried out  efficiently using  the  fast  Fourier transform algorithm implemented
in the efficient FFTW23 and cuFFT libraries on CPU and CUDA-enabled GPUs, respectively.

2.2 Potentials
The  electrostatic  potential  of a specimen determines how  transmitting  electrons  scatter and  thus connects
the properties of the material to the resulting images or diffraction patterns. Conversely, by directly analyzing scat-
tered intensities or comparing them to simulations of the specimen electrostatic potential, the properties of the
sample can be deduced. Fundamentally, the electrostatic potential is directly derived from the electron density of
the atoms in a specimen, which is described by their quantum mechanical many-body wave function.

Since this cannot be analytically solved except for the very simplest of molecules, various approximations have
been developed, such as early Hartree-Fock-Slater and Dirac-Fock formalisms. In the context of electron scat-
tering, these highly accurate but computationally extremely expensive techniques can be used to parametrize
(IAMs). However,  there  is  increasing  interest  in  a  fully ab  initio approach  to  calculating  the specimen
potential22. The most widely used and powerful such method is DFT, where the many-body problem of N elec-
trons with 3N spatial coordinates  is reduced to a variational solution for the three spatial coordinates of the
electron density.

While abTEM  is designed explicitly for ab initio potentials, IAM potentials can in many cases be sufficient
or useful: for example, typical annular dark-field contrast in STEM is dominated by nuclear scattering and thus

well described by the IAM, and in general, comparing images or diffraction patterns simulated with ab initio
potentials  to  the IAM  allows  the  effects  of  chemical bonding  to be  elucidated. Thus, abTEM  supports
common parametrized IAM potentials in addition to its integration with DFT methods.

2.3 Parametrized potentials
A potential parametrization, as pioneered by Doyle and Turner24, is a numerical  fit to atomic electron scatter-
ing factors calculated from  first principles, describing the radial dependence of the potential for each element.
abTEM supports two of the most accurate recent parametrizations: that by Lobato and Van Dyck25 (which is the
abTEM default) and by Kirkland8.

bination of Gaussians and Lorentzians to Dirac-Fock scattering  factors, providing a widely used and robust
parametrization that was distributed  digitally from 1998 onwards. In 2014, Lobato and Van Dyck improved
the quality of the  fit  further, using hydrogen’s analytical  non-relativistic electron scattering  factors as basis
functions to enable the correct inclusion of all physical constraints, providing to date the most accurate universal
neutral atom parameter set25. For a comparison of several parametrizations to each other as well as quantitative
experimental data for 2D materials, please see Ref. 6.

Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) is one of the most versatile and powerful experimental tools for the
imaging and diffraction of structures ranging from the micrometer scale with sub-Ångström resolution now rou-
tinely achievable in modern aberration corrected instruments. In TEM, information about the sample structure is
encoded in the scattering of the electron waves by the full electromagnetic potential of the specimen, which is domi-
nated by the atomic electrostatic potentials. These potentials include the contribution of the screened nuclear cores
as well as the valence electron density of the sample, and since valence electrons are responsible for binding the

The modern electron microscope should be an ideal tool for the high-resolution imaging of charge redistribution
caused by chemical bonding, but these measurements are a challenge because only a small fraction of the total elec-
trons in a material participate in bonding, and because the dense cores dominate the scattering signal. However,

Abstract:
While research on lightweight materials has been carried out for decades, it has become intensified with recent climate action initiatives leading pathways to net zero. Aluminum alloys are at the pinnacle of the light metal world, especially in the automotive and aerospace industries. This review intends to highlight recent developments in the processing, structure, and mechanical properties of structural Al-Si alloys to solve various pressing environmental issues via lightweighting strategies. With the excellent castability of Al-Si alloys, advancements in emerging casting methods and additive manufacturing processes have been summarized in relation to varying chemical compositions. Improvements in thermal stability and electrical conductivity, along with superior mechanical strength and fatigue resistance, are analyzed for advanced Al-Si alloys with the addition of other alloying elements. The role of Si morphology modification, along with particle distribution, size, and precipitation sequencing, is discussed in connection with the improvement of static and dynamic mechanical properties of the alloys. The physics-based damage mechanisms of fatigue failure under high-cycle and low-cycle fatigue loading are further elaborated for Al-Si alloys. The defect, porosity, and surface topography related to manufacturing processes and chemical compositions are also reviewed. Based on the gaps identified here, future research directions are suggested, including the usage of computational modeling of microstructures and the integration of artificial intelligence to produce mass-efficient and cost-effective solutions for the manufacturing of Al-Si alloys.

## pqac-00000012

From text 'zhang2025comparisonofkikuchi pages 1-6'.

Tian-cang Zhang, Lukas Berners, Jakub Holzer, and T. B. Britton. Comparison of kikuchi diffraction geometries in the scanning electron microscope. Apr 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matchar.2025.114853, doi:10.1016/j.matchar.2025.114853. This article has 14 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Winkelmann's dynamical diffraction simulation framework for Kikuchi patterns operates on three key assumptions. First, it separates initial inelastic scattering from subsequent elastic and coherent scattering. Second, it prioritizes reproducing small variations in intensity (pattern features) rather than absolute intensities, using simplified electron density calculations based on incident/outgoing beam directions, energy, and thickness. Third, it applies the reciprocity principle to transform the calculation into scattering of a plane wave from a detector point by the lattice, enabling the Bloch Wave approach to calculate the resulting wave function. Multiple crystal planes are incorporated and integrated over sufficient scattering thickness using Bethe perturbation theory, allowing the framework to handle the wide solid angles and multiple bands present in SEM-based Kikuchi diffraction patterns.

The excerpt discusses multiple machine learning approaches for EBSD pattern analysis. Traditional methods include Hough-based indexing, dictionary indexing (which requires simulating a master pattern for each phase), and spherical indexing. The paper focuses on few-shot transfer learning applied to classify electron backscatter diffraction patterns (EBSPs) into six space groups. Transfer learning starts from ImageNet pre-trained weights, which provides strong initial filters and allows rapid model convergence with fewer training images. ns prior to Bragg scattering affects the contrast and sharpness of Kikuchi

patterns, and higher energy loss occurs when there are larger interaction volumes,

longer electron trajectories and higher probability of inelastic scattering, resulting in

more blurred patterns. Acknowledging the ambiguous definitions of “depth resolution”

and “information depth” and the different approaches in experimental and simulation

works, previous studies showed that the energy spectrum of scattered electrons in the

EBSD geometry is much wider than that in the off-axis TKD geometry [2], and that the

depth resolution of TKD-in-SEM is in the order of 5-20 nm [3] or 20-80 nm [49,50] from

the exit surface of the sample, while for EBSD it may even reach around 100-150 nm

from the top surface of the bulk sample [51]. Findings of the present work are consistent

with these prior studies as experimental patterns and reconstructed stereograms from

EBSD suffers from a higher extent of blurring that is likely caused by a variation in the

electron energy of the detected electron across the screen. As for RKD, simulation work

has shown that electrons are on average from higher depths than in EBSD, and their



                                                                       25energy spectrum is even wider [52], both further contributing to pattern blurring and

band contrast inversion. This is compounded by the reduced yield of backscattered

electrons by approximately 3 times for Al [24]. These effects mean that energy filtering

for RKD is even more important that for the other geometries, so that only high energy

electrons are used to form useful patterns which are easy to interpret.


In terms of pattern contrast and subtle features, contrast inversion and E/D effects will

impact the relative intensity of features within the pattern, which require more detailed

simulations and pattern matching algorithms [26,39]. Overall, these may impact the

angular resolution of methods such as high-resolution EBSD, as well as the realistic

possibility of ‘single shot’ integrated digital image correlation methods [53,54], if they are

not properly considered in the analysis algorithms. It should also be noticed that E/D

effects, diffraction spots and unevenness of contrast and/or SNR of the gnomonic

patterns will be inherited to the reconstructed diffraction sphere and included in re-

projected gnomonic patterns, in what is likely a physically unrealistic manner. Two

examples are shown in Figure 6 to highlight these issues. The first example uses an

experimental EBSD pattern showing E/D effects in some bands. Applying symmetry

operations and overlapping patterns on the sphere caused the E/D effects to be

averaged out, so the reprojected gnomonic pattern does not have the same E/D effects

in the same bands. The second example shows that a reprojected pattern from an

averaged stereogram, which uses patterns from different sample thicknesses, fails to

reproduce thickness effects and the diffraction spots that are seen within the

experimental pattern.

This issue is important, as it changes the strategy required to generate the reference

Kikuchi sphere and we recommend that multiple patterns are used to generate the full

sphere such that the contribution of an individual feature (e.g. spots or E/D for a

particular band) is not inherited into the sphere and biases the precision of subsequent

analysis (e.g. offsetting the orientation recovered using a subsequent pattern matching

algorithm). However, these features may be very important for more demanding

applications such as direct pattern comparisons, strain mapping or full lattice parameter

determination. For example, in the case of on-axis TKD patterns, simulation of the full

pattern contrast must consider a wider range of dynamical scattering effects and should

be even more complex. To the authors’ knowledge, while it is possible to simulate the



                                                                       27features of on-axis TKD patterns (including E/D, background, anomalous absorption)

and diffraction spots separately with the same method [39] it is not yet possible to

reproduce these features together in the same simulated pattern properly. When it is

possible to join these different contributions, it is expected that the added features

significantly increase the computational complexity of any analysis method (and most

applications will work when these effects are suppressed through pattern processing).


Stereographic reconstructions. This work used a highly symmetric structure (cubic,

space group No. 225, Fm-3m) as the model material system as this simplifies the

reconstruction and analysis due the small size of the fundamental zone. For lower

symmetry structures and for highly textured samples, flexible placement of the detector

and sample tilt may help access certain zone axes or features on the patterns to ensure

that the complete diffraction sphere is accessed or that a particular high contrast feature

is shown (e.g. a pseudosymmetry zone axis), similar to the flexibility in detector

placement that is required for dark field X-ray microscopy [55]. For example, this can be

potentially useful for symmetry determination as was previously demonstrated in [56].


Energy filtering with direct electron detectors. The type of direct electron detectors

used in this work allows for energy filtering of incoming electrons during pattern capture.

Prior work has shown that this is useful for improving EBSD pattern quality (as has been

shown in [57]).

Abstract:
Mapping grain orientation in crystalline solids is essential to investigate the relationships between local microstructure and crystallography and interpret materials properties. One of the main techniques used to perform these studies is electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). Due to the limited measurement throughput, however, EBSD is not suitable for characterizing samples with long-range microstructure heterogeneity, nor for building large material libraries that include numerous specimens. We present a machine learning approach for high-throughput crystal orientation mapping, which relies on the optical technique called directional reflectance microscopy. We successfully apply our method on Inconel 718 specimens produced by additive manufacturing, which exhibit complex, spatially-varying microstructures. These results demonstrate that optical orientation mapping on a metal alloy is achievable. Since our method is data-driven, it can be easily extended to different alloy systems produced using different manufacturing processes.

{"answer": "## State of the Art in Physically Accurate Dynamical Simulation of EBSD/Kikuchi Master Patterns (2020–2026)

### 1. The Established Dynamical Bloch-Wave + Monte Carlo Approach (EMsoft/EMsoftOO)

The foundational approach for quantitatively accurate EBSD master pattern simulation rests on many-beam dynamical electron diffraction theory, as initially demonstrated by Winkelmann et al. (2007) and subsequently implemented in the open-source EMsoft package by Callahan and De Graef (2013). The methodology operates on three key physical assumptions as described by Zhang et al. (2025): (1) the initial inelastic scattering event is separated from subsequent elastic and coherent diffraction; (2) small variations in observed intensity (i.e., pattern features) are prioritized over absolute intensities, permitting simplifications in the electron number density as a function of beam direction, energy, and depth; and (3) the reciprocity principle is applied to transform the backscatter geometry into an equivalent problem of a plane wave emitting from a point on the detector being scattered by the crystal lattice, enabling the Bloch-wave formalism to calculate the resulting wave function (pqac-00000012).

Inclusion of many crystal planes is achieved via Bethe perturbation theory, which partitions reflections into "strong" and "weak" beams—critical because SEM-based Kikuchi patterns subtend wide solid angles containing many overlapping bands (pqac-00000012). The Monte Carlo component models the energy and depth distribution of backscattered electrons in the interaction volume, providing a physically motivated weighting of the dynamical diffraction signal as a function of electron energy loss and escape depth. Pascal et al. (2018) formalized the energy-weighted dynamical scattering simulation for multiple SEM diffraction modalities, and this approach was extended by Singh et al. (2019) to 2D and 3D quasicrystals and by Zhu and De Graef (2020) to interaction volumes containing lattice defects.

EMsoftOO represents the object-oriented modernization of the EMsoft codebase (originally Fortran-based), announced by De Graef (2025). It retains the same underlying physics—multi-beam Bloch-wave dynamical scattering with Monte Carlo electron transport—while providing a more modular, maintainable software architecture. EMsoft/EMsoftOO remains the **de facto open-source standard** for generating physically accurate EBSD master patterns and is widely used in the community for dictionary indexing (DI), where each experimental pattern is compared against a dictionary of simulated patterns projected from the master pattern for all sampled orientations (pqac-00000017).

### 2. Alternative and Newer Formalisms

**Winkelmann's Bloch-wave implementation and commercial integration.** Winkelmann et al. (2021) published a comprehensive treatment of Kikuchi pattern simulations for both backscattered and transmitted electrons. Their Bloch-wave dynamical simulation code, which also uses a reciprocity-based approach with strong-beam approximations, is implemented within Oxford Instruments' AztecCrystal MapSweeper software. Zhang et al. (2025) used this implementation with thresholds of d_hkl > 0.4 Å and I_hkl > 10% of I_max for the strong-beam selection, generating 1000×1000-pixel stereographic projections of the diffraction sphere at a single primary energy (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000003). This approach differs from EMsoft's fuller Monte Carlo energy-depth coupling but is production-ready within the commercial EBSD ecosystem for template-based pattern matching.

Alternative formalisms—multislice, S-matrix, DFT-informed potentials—are mature for TEM but have not been adapted to production EBSD backscatter geometry. ML/CNN methods accelerate indexing and classification but do not replace the physics-based forward model. The Python ecosystem (kikuchipy, diffsims, pyEBSDindex) provides excellent analysis and indexing tools but relies on EMsoft for dynamical master-pattern generation. For metallic alloy applications, dynamical simulation is essential for phase discrimination and precision analysis, while kinematical methods remain adequate for routine high-symmetry orientation mapping.

# Summary

This 2020 paper by Kaufmann et al. demonstrates convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for EBSD phase mapping. The authors highlight that "the Hough transform strips most of the information about the crystal structure and chemistry from the image," leading to misclassification of similar phases. They note that dictionary-based approaches using simulated patterns from software like "EMSoft" have been proposed as solutions. The paper presents CNN-based machine learning as an alternative pathway, stating that "machine learning coupled phase mapping" could work "as databases of EBSD patterns encompass an increasing number of the possible space groups, chemistry changes, and lattice parameter variations." The work represents "the first demonstration of such capabilities" for autonomous phase differentiation using raw diffraction pattern information rather than Hough-processed data.

# Summary

This excerpt discusses machine learning approaches to EBSD pattern classification rather than the physical simulation methods requested. It describes using convolutional neural networks with few-shot transfer learning (initialized from ImageNet weights) to classify electron backscattered patterns (EBSPs) into six space groups. The paper compares models trained from scratch versus transfer learning: scratch-trained models showed high initial validation loss (11.5 ± 2.5) by epoch 1, while transfer-learned models achieved lower training and validation losses (0.56 ± 0.02 and 0.52 ± 0.3, respectively) from the start, enabling faster convergence. The approach was tested on Ni₉₀Al₁₀ samples. However, **this excerpt does not address dynamical simulation methods** (Bloch-wave, multislice, scattering-matrix), open-source software implementations (EMsoft, kikuchipy, diffsims), or accuracy-versus-cost trade-offs for master pattern generation—the core topics of the question.

# Summary

This 2018 paper presents a **first-principles DFT-based method for calculating electron scattering factors** for transmission electron microscopy (TEM), not EBSD specifically. The authors use projector-augmented waves (PAW) formalism to recover exact frozen core electron density and calculate electrostatic potentials, avoiding expensive all-electron calculations while capturing bonding effects beyond the independent atom model (IAM).

Key technical contributions:
- Solves Poisson equation in two steps: smooth "pseudo" part (Eq. 1) across 3D grid, then atomic corrections (Eq. 2) on radial grids within augmentation spheres
- Implements approach via **PyQSTEM interface to QSTEM code** using **multislice propagation method**
- Demonstrates accuracy matching all-electron DFT at lower computational cost
- Shows bonding effects are measurable and detectable in HRTEM and diffraction patterns

The work addresses **first-principles/DFT-informed scattering-factor approaches** but focuses on transmission geometry rather than backscatter (EBSD) geometry, limiting direct applicability to the question's specific EBSD/Kikuchi pattern context.

# Summary

The excerpt discusses electron scattering simulation methods, primarily focusing on multislice algorithms and potential calculations rather than EBSD-specific dynamical approaches.

**Key points:**

1. **Multislice Algorithm**: The most common TEM image simulation method, with implementations across multiple codes. Recent developments include GPU acceleration and the PRISM algorithm for accelerating STEM simulations.

2. **Potentials**: Two main approaches—parametrized Indirect Atomic Model (IAM) potentials (Lobato and Van Dyck, Kirkland parametrizations) and ab initio DFT-based potentials for more accurate bonding descriptions.

3. **abTEM Implementation**: A pure-Python, open-source package (GPLv3) merging DFT with electron scattering simulations. Features multislice and PRISM algorithms with GPU support (NVIDIA CUDA/cuFFT, AMD support planned). Announced at M&M 2020, superseding PyQSTEM.

4. **Performance**: Despite pure Python implementation, abTEM achieves performance comparable to C/Fortran codes through effective open-source library utilization.

However, the excerpt does not address EBSD/Kikuchi patterns, dynamical Bloch-wave approaches, EMsoft, or machine-learning surrogates for EBSD indexing.

contexts.context: Winkelmann's dynamical diffraction simulation framework for Kikuchi patterns operates on three key assumptions. First, it separates initial inelastic scattering from subsequent elastic and coherent scattering. Second, it prioritizes reproducing small variations in intensity (pattern features) rather than absolute intensities, using simplified electron density calculations based on incident/outgoing beam directions, energy, and thickness. Third, it applies the reciprocity principle to transform the calculation into scattering of a plane wave from a detector point by the lattice, enabling the Bloch Wave approach to calculate the resulting wave function. Multiple crystal planes are incorporated and integrated over sufficient scattering thickness using Bethe perturbation theory, allowing the framework to handle the wide solid angles and multiple bands present in SEM-based Kikuchi diffraction patterns.

The paper also discusses dictionary-based approaches where simulated diffraction pattern libraries are compared with experimentally collected patterns using software like EMSoft. The authors suggest this machine learning methodology provides a path forward as EBSD pattern databases expand to encompass more space groups, chemistry variations, and lattice parameter variations.

The authors implement CNNs using TensorFlow and Keras API for classifying diffraction patterns, training on diffraction pattern data. The study employs transfer learning by comparing pseudo RGB transfer learning models against models trained from scratch. For model evaluation, they use precision and recall metrics calculated via Scikit-learn for each material and space group, with F1-score serving as a weighted harmonic metric particularly valuable when test images per class are variable. They employ Shapley values (SHAP) for model explainability to understand which image features positively or negatively correlate with class predictions. The training setup used early stopping with 15 epochs for validation loss convergence and weight decay of 1e-5, implemented on NVIDIA Titan V hardware. contexts.context: This paper presents an efficient few-shot machine learning approach for EBSD pattern classification using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transfer learning. The study compares two training approaches: training from scratch on grayscale images versus transfer learning using ImageNet pre-trained weights with 3-channel stacked images. Transfer learning demonstrates superior performance and efficiency, requiring only 26±3 epochs versus 50±12 epochs for the model trained from scratch, resulting in nearly one hour time savings per training event. Classification metrics show improved performance with transfer learning: 0.97 precision and 0.96 recall compared to 0.93 and 0.92 respectively for the from-scratch model. The authors emphasize that ImageNet-learned feature extractors are highly relevant to EBSD pattern classification, suggesting the general nature of these features transfers effectively to this specialized domain. The paper includes detailed visualization of learned filters and kernels, demonstrating that the models independently learn valuable edge detection operators and other feature extraction mechanisms suitable for EBSD pattern analysis.

contexts.context: abTEM performs electron scattering simulations using the multislice algorithm, which mathematically slices the potential into xy planes. It employs Projector-Augmented Wave (PAW) methods via the DFT code GPAW to obtain accurate ab initio all-electron electrostatic potentials derived from first principles calculations. The code implements two projection methods: finite numerical integrals (more accurate) and infinite integrals (faster). For large-scale STEM simulations, abTEM incorporates the PRISM algorithm, which expresses the electron probe as a plane-wave expansion and propagates individual plane-wave basis functions through the specimen independently. The total charge density combines explicitly computed valence wave functions, frozen core electron density from PAW projectors, and point-charge nuclei. Currently, abTEM uses only electrostatic potentials, though magnetic interactions are an emerging focus area.

Critically, "it is not yet possible to reproduce these features together in the same simulated pattern properly" for on-axis TKD, though individual features (E/D, background, spots) can be simulated separately.

**Reconstruction artifacts:** Multiple patterns are recommended for Kikuchi sphere generation to avoid biasing orientation analysis through inherited features like diffraction spots or E/D effects.

Question: In electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), 'the catch is the physics': kinematical (single-scattering) simulations get Kikuchi band positions right but not intensities, while quantitatively accurate patterns require full dynamical electron diffraction. What is the current state of the art (roughly 2020-2026) for physically accurate dynamical simulation of EBSD/Kikuchi master patterns and their implementations? Please cover: (1) the established dynamical Bloch-wave + Monte Carlo approach used by EMsoft/EMsoftOO (multi-beam dynamical scattering, Monte Carlo electron energy/depth distributions) and any recent methodological refinements; (2) alternative or newer formalisms such as multislice, scattering-matrix/S-matrix, reciprocity-based, or first-principles/DFT-informed scattering-factor approaches for backscatter geometries; (3) machine-learning / neural-network surrogates and GPU-accelerated methods that emulate or speed up dynamical pattern simulation and dictionary indexing; (4) the state of open-source, pure-Python or otherwise easily installable implementations (kikuchipy, diffsims, pyEMsoft, py4DSTEM, abTEM, etc.) and whether any now provide dynamical (not just kinematical) EBSD master patterns; and (5) practical accuracy-vs-cost trade-offs for dictionary indexing of metallic alloys (e.g. Al-Si). Cite specific papers, software, and authors, and note which approaches are production-ready versus research prototypes.

## State of the Art in Physically Accurate Dynamical Simulation of EBSD/Kikuchi Master Patterns (2020–2026)

### 1. The Established Dynamical Bloch-Wave + Monte Carlo Approach (EMsoft/EMsoftOO)

The foundational approach for quantitatively accurate EBSD master pattern simulation rests on many-beam dynamical electron diffraction theory, as initially demonstrated by Winkelmann et al. (2007) and subsequently implemented in the open-source EMsoft package by Callahan and De Graef (2013). The methodology operates on three key physical assumptions as described by Zhang et al. (2025): (1) the initial inelastic scattering event is separated from subsequent elastic and coherent diffraction; (2) small variations in observed intensity (i.e., pattern features) are prioritized over absolute intensities, permitting simplifications in the electron number density as a function of beam direction, energy, and depth; and (3) the reciprocity principle is applied to transform the backscatter geometry into an equivalent problem of a plane wave emitting from a point on the detector being scattered by the crystal lattice, enabling the Bloch-wave formalism to calculate the resulting wave function (zhang2025comparisonofkikuchi pages 1-6).

Inclusion of many crystal planes is achieved via Bethe perturbation theory, which partitions reflections into "strong" and "weak" beams—critical because SEM-based Kikuchi patterns subtend wide solid angles containing many overlapping bands (zhang2025comparisonofkikuchi pages 1-6). The Monte Carlo component models the energy and depth distribution of backscattered electrons in the interaction volume, providing a physically motivated weighting of the dynamical diffraction signal as a function of electron energy loss and escape depth. Pascal et al. (2018) formalized the energy-weighted dynamical scattering simulation for multiple SEM diffraction modalities, and this approach was extended by Singh et al. (2019) to 2D and 3D quasicrystals and by Zhu and De Graef (2020) to interaction volumes containing lattice defects.

EMsoftOO represents the object-oriented modernization of the EMsoft codebase (originally Fortran-based), announced by De Graef (2025). It retains the same underlying physics—multi-beam Bloch-wave dynamical scattering with Monte Carlo electron transport—while providing a more modular, maintainable software architecture. EMsoft/EMsoftOO remains the **de facto open-source standard** for generating physically accurate EBSD master patterns and is widely used in the community for dictionary indexing (DI), where each experimental pattern is compared against a dictionary of simulated patterns projected from the master pattern for all sampled orientations (kaufmann2020phasemappingin pages 1-2).

### 2. Alternative and Newer Formalisms

**Winkelmann's Bloch-wave implementation and commercial integration.** Winkelmann et al. (2021) published a comprehensive treatment of Kikuchi pattern simulations for both backscattered and transmitted electrons. Their Bloch-wave dynamical simulation code, which also uses a reciprocity-based approach with strong-beam approximations, is implemented within Oxford Instruments' AztecCrystal MapSweeper software. Zhang et al. (2025) used this implementation with thresholds of d_hkl > 0.4 Å and I_hkl > 10% of I_max for the strong-beam selection, generating 1000×1000-pixel stereographic projections of the diffraction sphere at a single primary energy (zhang2025comparisonofkikuchi pages 15-20). This approach differs from EMsoft's fuller Monte Carlo energy-depth coupling but is production-ready within the commercial EBSD ecosystem for template-based pattern matching.

**Multislice approaches.** The multislice algorithm—standard for TEM/STEM simulation—has been explored for EBSD geometry (Liu et al., 2016, compared two multislice methods for EBSD pattern simulation). However, the multislice method is fundamentally designed for forward-scattering (transmission) geometries and requires substantial adaptation for the wide-angle backscatter geometry of EBSD. Xiao et al. (2026) recently reported experimentally validated multislice simulations of electron diffraction patterns, though primarily for transmission geometries. To the authors' knowledge, no production-ready multislice code currently generates full dynamical EBSD master patterns.

**S-matrix and PRISM methods.** Scattering-matrix (S-matrix) approaches, as discussed by Ophus (2019) in the context of 4D-STEM, and the PRISM algorithm for accelerating STEM simulations, represent important algorithmic advances for transmission electron microscopy but have not been adapted to the EBSD backscatter master-pattern problem in production codes.

**DFT-informed scattering factors.** Susi et al. (2019) developed an efficient method for generating ab initio electrostatic potentials using the projector-augmented wave (PAW) formalism, enabling DFT-derived scattering factors that account for chemical bonding effects neglected by the independent atom model (IAM) (susi2019efficientfirstprinciples pages 1-3). The abTEM code (Madsen and Susi, 2021) integrates these DFT potentials with multislice simulations and supports both CPU and GPU acceleration (madsen2021theabtemcode pages 3-5, madsen2021theabtemcode pages 1-3). However, abTEM is explicitly a **transmission** electron microscopy simulation code—it supports HRTEM, STEM, CBED, 4D-STEM, and ptychography, but the retrieved evidence contains no documentation of EBSD backscatter master-pattern generation capability (madsen2021theabtemcode pages 10-12, madsen2021theabtemcode pages 12-15, madsen2021theabtemcode pages 15-17). DFT-informed potentials remain an area where future integration with Bloch-wave EBSD codes could refine accuracy for materials where bonding effects are measurable.

**Inelastic scattering treatments.** Mendis et al. (2020) and Vos and Winkelmann (2019) investigated the roles of multiple elastic and inelastic scattering and energy-resolved contrast in Kikuchi diffraction, contributing to the theoretical understanding of how thermal diffuse scattering, plasmon losses, and phonon scattering affect EBSD pattern formation. These treatments inform improvements to the energy weighting in dynamical simulations but have not yet been incorporated into a distinct production simulation code.

### 3. Machine-Learning / Neural-Network Surrogates and GPU-Accelerated Methods

Several groups have applied deep learning to EBSD pattern analysis, though primarily for **classification and indexing** rather than for replacing the physical forward model:

- **CNN-based phase mapping:** Kaufmann et al. (2020) demonstrated that convolutional neural networks (CNNs, specifically the Xception architecture) can autonomously recognize phases by crystal symmetry, chemistry, and lattice parameters from EBSD patterns, outperforming traditional Hough-based methods for phase discrimination in multiphase materials (kaufmann2020phasemappingin pages 2-3, kaufmann2020phasemappingin pages 1-2).

- **Few-shot transfer learning:** Kaufmann et al. (2021) showed that transfer learning from ImageNet pre-trained weights enables efficient EBSD pattern classification with far fewer training examples (few-shot learning), achieving 0.97 precision and 0.96 recall for space-group classification with substantially faster convergence than training from scratch (kaufmann2021efficientfewshotmachine pages 2-3, kaufmann2021efficientfewshotmachine pages 3-4).

- **Orientation extraction by CNNs:** Jha et al. (2018) applied CNNs for extracting grain orientations directly from polycrystalline EBSD patterns, and Ding (2022) further explored ML-based orientation determination (kaufmann2021efficientfewshotmachine pages 10-11).

- **GPU-accelerated indexing:** The pyEBSDindex package (Rowenhorst, Callahan, and Ånes, 2024) provides GPU-accelerated Radon-transform-based band detection and EBSD orientation determination, dramatically speeding up the indexing step. This tool is production-ready and open-source but is an **indexer**, not a master-pattern generator.

It is important to note that current ML approaches function as **surrogates for the search/classification step** of the EBSD workflow—they do not replace the authoritative generation of dynamical master patterns by physics-based simulation. No published work in the 2020–2026 window demonstrates a neural network that generates quantitatively accurate dynamical EBSD master patterns from first principles, though ML-based denoising and pattern enhancement (e.g., Andrews et al., 2023) improve the quality of experimental patterns fed into physics-based indexing pipelines.

Key observations:

- **kikuchipy** (Ånes et al.) is a mature, pip-installable Python package for EBSD pattern processing, background correction, and analysis. It can load and project master patterns generated by EMsoft but does **not itself contain a dynamical Bloch-wave simulation engine** for generating EBSD master patterns. It provides kinematical approximations and geometrical projections.

- **diffsims** (pyxem ecosystem) provides kinematical diffraction simulation objects and is useful for electron diffraction geometry but does not produce dynamical EBSD master patterns.

- **orix** (Johnstone et al., 2020) handles crystal orientations and symmetry operations, complementing the above tools.

- **pyEBSDindex** is focused on fast GPU-accelerated indexing, not pattern simulation.

- **abTEM** (Madsen and Susi, 2021) is the most physically sophisticated pure-Python simulation code, supporting multislice dynamical diffraction with DFT-informed potentials and GPU acceleration, but it is designed exclusively for TEM/STEM transmission geometries and does not currently support EBSD backscatter master-pattern generation (madsen2021theabtemcode pages 3-5, madsen2021theabtemcode pages 1-3).

- **pyEMsoft** provides Python bindings to EMsoft's Fortran-based dynamical simulation routines and is the closest route to dynamical EBSD master patterns from a Python interface, though it requires compiling the underlying EMsoft libraries.

In summary, as of 2026, **no pure-Python, pip-installable package independently generates dynamical EBSD master patterns**. The practical workflow remains: use EMsoft (or EMsoftOO) to generate master patterns, then use kikuchipy/orix/pyEBSDindex for downstream analysis, projection, and indexing.

### 5. Accuracy-vs-Cost Trade-offs for Dictionary Indexing of Metallic Alloys

For metallic alloys such as Al-Si systems, several practical considerations govern the choice of simulation approach:

- **Kinematical simulations** correctly predict Kikuchi band positions (governed by Bragg's law and crystal geometry) and can suffice for basic orientation indexing via Hough-transform methods in high-symmetry, single-phase materials. However, they fail to reproduce the relative intensities of bands, the fine structure at zone axes, and excess-deficiency (E/D) effects (zhang2025comparisonofkikuchi pages 1-6).

- **Dynamical simulations** are necessary for (a) resolving pseudosymmetry ambiguities (e.g., distinguishing tetragonal from cubic phases), (b) phase discrimination in multi-phase alloys where crystal structures are similar (e.g., distinguishing Al matrix from Si precipitates, or ferrite from martensite in steels), (c) high-resolution EBSD strain mapping that requires accurate simulated reference patterns, and (d) template-based pattern matching that relies on physically correct intensity distributions (kaufmann2020phasemappingin pages 1-2, zhang2025comparisonofkikuchi pages 25-30).

- **Computational cost:** Generating a single dynamical EBSD master pattern with EMsoft typically requires minutes to hours on modern hardware depending on the number of reflectors and angular resolution. Dictionary indexing then requires projecting this master pattern for O(10^5–10^6) orientations and comparing each to the experimental pattern, which is computationally intensive but has been made tractable by GPU acceleration and spherical indexing methods. For an Al-Si alloy, one would generate separate master patterns for the Al (FCC, space group 225) and Si (diamond cubic, space group 227) phases.

- **Practical recommendation:** For routine orientation mapping of well-known high-symmetry metallic phases, Hough-based indexing with kinematical band tables remains fast and adequate. When phase discrimination, pseudosymmetry resolution, or precision orientation refinement is needed—common in Al-Si alloys containing multiple intermetallic phases—dynamical simulation via EMsoft combined with dictionary or template-based indexing provides measurably superior accuracy at the cost of longer setup and computation times. Zhang et al. (2025) demonstrated that dynamical template matching using the Winkelmann Bloch-wave approach (implemented in AztecCrystal MapSweeper) successfully determined orientations across multiple Kikuchi diffraction geometries for Al samples, with reconstructed diffraction spheres closely matching the dynamical simulations, though some differences remained at zone axes and HOLZ rings (zhang2025comparisonofkikuchi pages 30-35, zhang2025comparisonofkikuchi pages 25-30).

### Summary

The state of the art for physically accurate dynamical EBSD simulation remains firmly grounded in the Bloch-wave + reciprocity + Bethe perturbation formalism, with EMsoft/EMsoftOO (De Graef group) and Winkelmann's implementation (now in Oxford AztecCrystal) as the two production-ready engines. Alternative formalisms—multislice, S-matrix, DFT-informed potentials—are mature for TEM but have not been adapted to production EBSD backscatter geometry. ML/CNN methods accelerate indexing and classification but do not replace the physics-based forward model. The Python ecosystem (kikuchipy, diffsims, pyEBSDindex) provides excellent analysis and indexing tools but relies on EMsoft for dynamical master-pattern generation. For metallic alloy applications, dynamical simulation is essential for phase discrimination and precision analysis, while kinematical methods remain adequate for routine high-symmetry orientation mapping.

info.query: In electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), 'the catch is the physics': kinematical (single-scattering) simulations get Kikuchi band positions right but not intensities, while quantitatively accurate patterns require full dynamical electron diffraction. What is the current state of the art (roughly 2020-2026) for physically accurate dynamical simulation of EBSD/Kikuchi master patterns and their implementations? Please cover: (1) the established dynamical Bloch-wave + Monte Carlo approach used by EMsoft/EMsoftOO (multi-beam dynamical scattering, Monte Carlo electron energy/depth distributions) and any recent methodological refinements; (2) alternative or newer formalisms such as multislice, scattering-matrix/S-matrix, reciprocity-based, or first-principles/DFT-informed scattering-factor approaches for backscatter geometries; (3) machine-learning / neural-network surrogates and GPU-accelerated methods that emulate or speed up dynamical pattern simulation and dictionary indexing; (4) the state of open-source, pure-Python or otherwise easily installable implementations (kikuchipy, diffsims, pyEMsoft, py4DSTEM, abTEM, etc.) and whether any now provide dynamical (not just kinematical) EBSD master patterns; and (5) practical accuracy-vs-cost trade-offs for dictionary indexing of metallic alloys (e.g. Al-Si). Cite specific papers, software, and authors, and note which approaches are production-ready versus research prototypes.
